In the organization of the Government our fathers found slavery a troublesome question and from that day to the present whenever it has been treated as a national question, and made the subject of federal legislation, it has disturbed the harmony of our society, and endangered the perpetuity of the Union. After struggle of more than half century, an adjustment was made, by the adoption of the compromise measures of 1850, which was acquiesced in by the different sections of the Union, and brought peace to the country. That was the last great act of Clay, of Cass and of Webster. For three years the great States of the North had demanded that all the country which we had acquired from Mexico should be free, and that slavery should for ever be excluded therefrom, by Congressional legislation; and the fifteen States of the South claimed it as common country, open to the people of the South with their property, as it was to the men of the North with their property. That was a mighty controversy, fought between great parties, arraying the States of the Union against each other, and to settle it Henry Clay returned from private life to the Senate of the United States. He was met by good and able men from the North and from the South. Party distinctions and prejudices were laid aside and forgotten, and the common good controlled the hearts and guided the judgments of patriotic men. As early as 1813, and again in 1850, it was proposed to divide the country between the North and South, by extending the Missouri Compromise line over it, giving to the North the largest and most valuable portion; but that proposition was rejected, and that principle of legislature repudiated. The North gave a large vote against it, saying we will not sustain such an adjustment. We have all seen, and that quite lately, that workmen will insist on as high wages as they can get; employers will do the same. If laborers should become so plentiful and work so scarce here that men could be had to work all day for ten cents, no sensible employer would give eleven; it would not be wise, or prudent or fair. The workmen might complain and strike and riot; the Legislature might make laws, and demagogues prate; but the end of it would be that the employers would stick to their offer of ten cents, and the workmen would take it. All attempts to disturb the natural balance of supply and demand and wages, either by Legislative acts or popular violence, only create mischief and never achieve any beneficial end.

We have sufficient faith in the common sense of the workingmen to believe that knowledge of these cardinal truths would induce them to abandon their present course, were it not for the pernicious action of another class of society. While the workmen are refusing to work for 10s a day, and idling their time in the Park, the rich are busy right and left in devising extensive charities. One man sets apart a portion of the enormous wealth he has gained by feeding the social extravagance of past years, to setting up a soup kitchen, and giving soup to twelve hundred men every day. Another prominent member of society hits upon a clever little scheme for presenting hundreds of cotton dresses to the poor. Others contrive a great ball, whereby thousands are placed in fund to be given in charity. Others contribute on to this, another to that charitable institution; and thus, within the last month or so, probably something like one hundred thousand dollars have been raised or spent in this aim in this city alone.

It is this aim of giving which causes the strikes and the obstinacy of workmen.

It is vain to flatter ourselves; mankind does not change; if you would move the masses you must lead them by their interest. "Attack them by the bellies" said the Duke of Wellington to the Prime Minister of England, on the occasion of riot; and so the bakers' stores were shut, and the rioters went home. Let us take hint from the Duke. Suppose we turn these emigrants out of doors—the fellows who turned up their noses at twelve shillings a day—let them sleep night in the Park, and go without breakfast next morning. Suppose we try little of the same regimen with the longshoremen, and the other stout fellows who won't submit to diminution of wages. What would be the result?

Why they would laugh at us. Bill Guys, he won't submit to be cut down, and won't work at all; so he has a bowl of hot soup at Mr. Steward's and smokes his pipe sulkily in the Park the rest of the day. Pat is ready to knock any man down who wants him to work for less than he got last year; he has his eye on Mr. Gerard, and intends to see that he gets his share of the ten thousand dollars given for the poor—for the poor, mind you, which means Pat and his friends—at the Academy ball. Fritz has been living very comfortably at such a soup house for some days; and on the whole he is satisfied with the arrangements despite the want of pepper in the soup, of which he complains loudly—and will continue to dine there for the present. In the afternoon Fritz discourses on communism of a lager beer saloon.

We challenge denial of the truth of this picture. In plain words, you have provided the poor with food without work, and now, you are preposterously expecting them to do so.

her cares and duties—and should make any
sacrifice or denial on her own part, rather
than they should feel uncared for, unloved,
or burden on her time and attention.


They should be made to realize that they
are cherished within her heart of hearts,
and that their comfort and well being are
the objects of her daily solicitude, the main
spring of all her acts.


Thus feeling, they will have little or no
desire for resorts of pleasure beyond the
fireside; and as they advance in age, will
be protected in a great measure from the
temptations of the world and outdoor life,
and in long after years will look back upon
that mother's tenderness as the safeguard
from many sins.


And if that mother should have gone to
rest, there will be a halo round her memo
ry that will light them on through many a
darksome path, incite them on to many good
deeds, and keep them free from vice.


Let it, therefore, be the pleasant task
of the mother to keep the sunny brow of
childhood undimmed as far as lies within
her power, for clouds will come full soon
enough to darken o'er their sky.


We can imagine no sadder scene, no
greater object of pity, than a neglected,
lonely child, uncheered by caressing kiss or
approving smile from its cold, disinterested
mother.—Rural New York.

IRONTON, June 20, 1855.
Messrs. Editors:

Messrs. Peters, James & Co., in an article published in your paper yesterday deny that there ever was a contract existing between themselves and the Boilers as to Cincinnati prices, and ask why the parties to such contract are not named. We will try to answer their inquiry.

In the first place we do say that such a contract was made and agreed to by both the boilers and Mr. Wm. Powell, the manager of the mill. The meeting of sympathisers with Rev. Mr. Dennis whose slave, Rosetta, was taken from him and freed while passing through Ohio was held at Jefferson County. A series of speeches made by Nathaniel Wolf, Sierra, William, and Joshua T. Butt, and a series of resolutions adopted.

The first RESOLUTION enters the dire interest course of Rev. Mr. Dennis. The third is addressed to Hon. H. H. Robinson, the United States Marshal. The fifth asks the Legislature of Kentucky to reimburse Rev. Mr. Dennis for his losses, and suit brought, if necessary, to the Supreme Court of the Union. The rest we copy entire:

1st. Our right of transit through the free States with our slaves is a perfect right under the Constitution of the Union.

2nd. That the people of every county of Kentucky and of the city of Louisville are earnestly entreated in meetings to express their opinions on the above going resolutions.

3rd. That the editors of each newspaper in Kentucky are respectfully requested to publish these proceedings.

4th. That the people of Kentucky hold themselves ready as they ever have done to aid the cause in maintaining the supremacy of the Constitution and Laws, and the direction it must come from whatever quarter it may.

5th. Wm. T. Butt, Samuel Geiger, George Hancock and Edward Y. Robb, appointed corresponding committee, for the purpose of calling the attention of other counties in this State to this matter, and invoking their aid by calling mass meetings of the people, and sending petitions to the next legislature.

The committee are also instructed to visit them on the second Monday of the session of the Legislature, and lay their resolutions and proceedings before them.
